new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is stated in any accessible source. Nalca is reported (via the unpublished Rule, Rule & Cutting 1972 alphabet-and-grammar statement) to have both tone with two levels (high and low) and distinctive, i.e. contrastive, stress, neither of which is marked in the practical (New Testament) orthography. Heeschen 1978: 12–13 independently reports 'tones are said to be phonemic in Nalca and Kosarek (Bromley 1973:15 and Rule and Cutting)', says he found no minimal pair in Nalca, and derives the Nalca high tone / stress from syllable contraction (Nalca ampum [am'pʰóm] 'yesterday' < *ambotum, stress on the contracted final syllable); Bromley 1973: 15 says the Naltja language 'is clearly tonal, with two contrastive levels demonstrated (Bromley ms)'. So: tonal (2 levels, contested by Heeschen) plus lexically distinctive stress, location undescribed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Heeschen 1978: 13 restricts the tonal contrasts to 'a very limited set of the vocabulary' (contracted disyllables and words with a lost final glottal stop).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (orthographic words of the NT text). The one Nalca form with stress marked, Heeschen 1978: 12 ampum [am'pʰóm], is a citation form. Wälchli also notes a word-final suprasegmental glottal feature (written ') that is independent of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern the same variety: Nalca = Hmanggona = 'the language spoken at Naltja' (Bromley 1973) = the Goliath/Kim-Jal-family language of the Naltja area (Rule et al. 1972's title; 'Kimjal' was Sadlier's name for the family and is not the Korupun Kimyal language) = Glottolog nalc1240 / ISO nlc. Heeschen 1992: 467 places Nalca 'probably' with the south-west Mek group (Korapun, Sela). The Wälchli/Svärd data are from the Nalca New Testament translation.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Silent on stress, tone and phonology in general: the thesis is a morphosyntactic analysis of the Nalca New Testament as a parallel text (word order, verbs, nouns, case, noun classes, pronouns, numerals, questions, wordlist). The only 'stress' hits are the verb 'stressed that'. downloaded via the Internet Archive copy of the DiVA PDF (DiVA refused all connections by automated download).

sources.note: No statement about Nalca. p. 470: 'In Eipomek and in the dialects east of Eipomek, accent is phonemic. Angguruk places the accent on the last syllable, and the Yale language tends to place it on the last syllable.' Nalca is placed 'probably' in the south-west Korapun–Sela group (p. 467). downloaded via Internet Archive copy of the Brill/KITLV OA PDF (brill.com could not be reached by automated download).
